card.name: Arjuna Nritham
card.tagline: Kerala's ritual peacock dance honoring Bhadrakali through martial rhythms.
card.profile: Arjuna Nritham, also known as Mayilpeeli Thookkam, is a ritual dance tradition from south Kerala performed primarily in Bhagavathy temples. Practised by men of the Ezhava, Ashari, and Kollan communities, the art form mirrors the story of Arjuna propitiating goddess Bhadrakali. Dancers wear striking peacock-feather skirts around the waist alongside green face paint and ornate headgear. Accompanied by chenda drums and ilathalam cymbals, performers execute martial movements derived from Kalarippayattu across all-night rituals.
card.insight: Dancers paint their faces green and explain complex percussion rhythms to the temple audience before executing Kalarippayattu-style footwork all night long.

card.profile_long:
Arjuna Nritham, also documented as Mayilpeeli Thookkam, originates in the temple traditions of south Kerala, notably within the Kottayam and Alappuzha districts. The dance tradition is linked to the epic Mahabharatha, wherein Arjuna—recognized as a skilled warrior, singer, and dancer—is said to have offered a devotional performance to appease goddess Bhadrakali. Practised primarily by men of the Ezhava community, alongside performers from the Ashari and Kollan communities, the dance functions as a sacred ritual presentation within Bhagavathy temple grounds.

The dance form itself is known as Pyattu, characterized by physical movement patterns closely related to Kalarippayattu martial techniques. Performances take place across all-night ritual events, presented either solo or in pairs. A distinctive feature of the tradition is the structure of the accompanying music: strictly rhythm-based songs called Kavithangal present narratives from the Hindu Puranas. Each Kavitham is composed to align with a specific rhythmic structure. Prior to singing each piece, the dancers explain the technical intricacies of the rhythm to the audience, detailing how that specific meter translates directly into physical dance steps.

The visual presence of an Arjuna Nritham dancer is defined by elaborate ritual ornamentation designed to emulate the appearance of Arjuna. Dancers paint their faces green, wear prominent headgear designated as Nettipattom, and fasten a characteristic lower garment made of peacock feathers around the waist. This peacock-feather garment, called mayilppeeli, is tied around the hips in a fashion similar to the uduthukettu waist-cloth worn in Kathakali dance-drama. Percussion ensembles supporting the performance feature traditional Kerala instruments, including the chenda, talachenda, and ilathalam cymbals.

As a ritual art form embedded in temple worship, Arjuna Nritham maintains specific community traditions across generations in south Kerala. The performance serves both as a devotional offering to Bhadrakali and as a preservation of traditional percussion theory, vocal narrative, and martial physical training.

മഹാഭാരത കഥയുമായി ബന്ധപ്പെട്ട ഈ കലാരൂപം, അനുരഞ്ജനകല, അനുഷ്ഠാനകല, ആയോധനകല, മയിൽപ്പീലിതൂക്കം എന്നീ പേരുകളിലും അറിയപ്പെടുന്നു. ദേവീ ക്ഷേത്രങ്ങളിൽ "തൂക്കം" എന്ന നേർച്ച ഉത്സവത്തിന്റെ ഭാഗമായിട്ടാണ് ഈ കലാരൂപം അവതരിപ്പിച്ച് വരുന്നത്‌

card.sacred_note: Arjuna Nritham is a sacred ritual dance performed in Bhagavathy temples to propitiate goddess Bhadrakali. Outsiders should respect temple customs and refrain from disrupting all-night ritual procedures.

sections.origins_and_history: Arjuna Nritham, also called Mayilpeeli Thookkam, is rooted in the Bhagavathy temple traditions of south Kerala. The dance refers to the Mahabharatha legend in which Arjuna propitiates goddess Bhadrakali through a devotional performance. The art form has been preserved and transmitted through generations by men of the Ezhava community, as well as the Ashari and Kollan communities, predominantly in Kottayam and Alappuzha districts.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance movements are known as Pyattu and draw directly from the martial techniques of Kalarippayattu. Executed solo or in pairs during all-night performances, the dance is strictly tied to rhythmic songs called Kavithangal. Dancers verbally explain the specific rhythmic structure of each song to the gathered audience before physically translating those drum patterns into stepping and stance sequences.
sections.music_and_instruments: Music for Arjuna Nritham centers on Kavithangal, rhythm-driven vocal compositions detailing stories from the Hindu Puranas. Musical accompaniment is provided by percussion instruments characteristic of Kerala temple arts, specifically the chenda, talachenda, and ilathalam (cymbals).
sections.costume_and_setting: Performances occur in Bhagavathy temples. Dancers wear green facial makeup, ornate headgear known as Nettipattom, and a distinctive lower body garment crafted from peacock feathers (mayilppeeli) fastened around the waist in the manner of Kathakali's uduthukettu.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: The dance is performed as an all-night devotional ritual to propitiate goddess Bhadrakali. The costume and facial cosmetics are designed to evoke the hero Arjuna performing his act of devotion.
sections.regional_variants: The practice is primarily prevalent across Bhagavathy temples in the Kottayam and Alappuzha districts of south Kerala.
sections.lineage: Historically practiced and maintained by male members of the Ezhava, Ashari, and Kollan communities of south Kerala.

claims.text: Mayilpeeli Thookkam also called Arjuna Nritham is a ritual dance of Kerala primarily performed by men of the Ezhava community, and is prevalent in the Bhagavathy temples of south Kerala.
The dance references the Mahabharatha where Arjuna propitiated goddess Bhadrakali through a devotional presentation.
Performers wear green face paint, headgear called Nettipattom, and a peacock feather garment around the waist.
The dance is known as Pyattu with movements similar to Kalarippayattu techniques performed all night solo or in pairs.
Rhythmic songs called Kavithangal present puranic stories and dancers explain the rhythm intricacies before each song.
Musical accompaniment comprises percussion instruments like chenda, talachenda, and ilathalam.
The tradition is also practiced by the Ashari and Kollan communities in Kottayam and Alappuzha districts.
